profiles.meeting_scenario: At a large academic medical center, the diagnostic safety workgroup has noticed that its first quarter review of physician-reported missed and delayed diagnoses does not resemble the published pattern from a well-known multi-institution survey: the hospital's local data show far fewer testing-phase errors and many more clinician-assessment errors than expected. This troubleshooting meeting is between the physician leading diagnostic safety review and the quality informatics specialist who manages incident-report abstraction. The immediate agenda is to figure out why the internal case classifications look off, determine whether the issue is in the taxonomy workflow rather than in the underlying cases, and agree on a practical fix before the next patient safety committee report. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for re-reviewing a subset of reports and updating the reporting process so the hospital's diagnostic error trends are interpretable.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Hospitalist and Diagnostic Safety Physician Lead
members.expertise: Diagnostic error review, peer case analysis, inpatient and ED handoff failures
members.background: Lena is an internal medicine hospitalist who was asked by the chief medical officer to build the hospital's first formal diagnostic safety review process using published diagnostic error taxonomies and physician-submitted cases.
members.private_state: She wants the next committee report to show clinically credible categories that physicians will trust, and she is worried that if the classification logic feels administratively driven, frontline clinicians will stop submitting cases.
hidden_assumptions: A 'follow-up failure' starts after an abnormal result is already available in the chart and a clinician does not act on it promptly.
When people refer to 'the March colon cancer cases,' they mean the three physician-reviewed delayed-diagnosis cases discussed in last month's diagnostic safety huddle.
A case is not really 'closed' until the diagnostic breakdown point has been agreed upon by clinical reviewers, even if the reporting software status says complete.
A 'second pass with the taxonomy' means targeted physician adjudication of the ambiguous or high-harm cases, not re-abstracting every record from scratch.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Patient safety reporting systems, chart abstraction, taxonomy field mapping, committee dashboard preparation
members.background: Priya is a nurse informaticist who administers the hospital's RLDatix event workflow, converts narrative reports into structured categories, and prepares monthly trend summaries for quality committees.
members.private_state: She wants to prevent another late dashboard revision cycle and is concerned about keeping abstraction consistent across reviewers so the reporting pipeline remains auditable and on schedule.
hidden_assumptions: A 'follow-up failure' includes any broken loop after suspicion begins, including missed scheduling, lost outreach, uncompleted downstream testing, or patient non-completion if the system did not close the loop.
When someone mentions 'the March colon cancer cases,' they mean the three records dated March in the dashboard export, regardless of when the patient encounter occurred or where the case originated.
A case is 'closed' once all required data fields, harm score, and event status are finalized in RLDatix, even if reviewers still have nuanced differences in causal framing.
A 'second pass with the taxonomy' means a standardized re-abstraction workflow applied by the abstraction team to the entire flagged set so the database remains internally consistent.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a follow-up failure
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should recode the 'follow-up failures' correctly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ortiz means cases where an abnormal test result was posted but the responsible clinician failed to acknowledge or act on it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya means any diagnostic loop that did not reach completion, including unscheduled colonoscopy, unreturned call, or patient never getting the next test.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are common in diagnostic safety work and sound fully compatible in casual discussion, so the phrase feels precise enough even though one meaning is narrower and clinician-centered while the other is broader and system-centered.

misalignment_points.topic: Which colon cancer cases are being discussed
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the March colon cancer cases' as a shared example set.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ortiz is thinking of the three delayed colorectal cancer cases brought to physician peer review last month, all tied to abnormal FIT results with delayed colonoscopy referral.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya is thinking of the three records timestamped in the March dashboard extract under colorectal cancer, which include one pathology backlog case entered in March but originating from January and one miscoded surveillance case.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The count happens to match, both recently handled a trio of colon cancer-related cases, and neither has reason to suspect the other is anchoring on a different indexing scheme than their own.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to close the backlog
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'close the backlog' before the next safety committee report.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ortiz means the clinically important cases should have settled causal categories so the testing-vs-assessment trend is trustworthy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya means all pending records should have completed required fields and final statuses so the dashboard can be issued on time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital quality work, 'closed' naturally carries both an operational and an analytic sense, and because both are trying to be efficient, neither notices that they are using different completion standards.

misalignment_points.topic: What a second pass with the taxonomy involves
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to do 'a second pass with the taxonomy' this week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ortiz assumes this means brief physician adjudication of only the discordant or major-harm cases to sharpen the category boundaries.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya assumes this means her team will re-abstract the entire flagged batch using the full structured taxonomy and harm-scoring workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Second-pass review is a routine quality-control phrase, and each person's default method fits their role so naturally that the procedural difference does not sound like a separate decision requiring explicit discussion.

turns.inner_thought: Our quarter-one pattern looks wrong. In the published diagnostic safety literature, testing and follow-up problems usually show up much more often. If our local report says mostly clinician assessment issues, I worry we're coding clinically obvious test-tracking breakdowns into the wrong bins. If physicians see that, they'll decide this is an administrative exercise and stop submitting cases.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I've been looking at the quarter-one review, and the split doesn't make sense to me compared with the benchmark data. We're showing a lot fewer testing-phase breakdowns and a lot more assessment issues than I'd expect. I wanted to step through where the classification might be drifting.

turns.inner_thought: The pipeline itself has been straightforward: physician narratives come in, we abstract them into the RLDatix fields, assign the taxonomy categories, and queue anything incomplete. My immediate problem is operational. I still have records with pending fields and statuses, and if we don't close the backlog before the committee packet locks, I'll be back in revision mode again.
turns.utterance: From the workflow side, we've been taking the physician-submitted narratives, mapping them into the RLDatix fields, and then assigning the taxonomy categories from there. Where it's gotten messy is volume and timing. We still have a backlog that needs to be closed before the committee packet goes out, so some of what you're seeing may reflect cases that haven't fully settled in the system yet.

turns.inner_thought: What keeps jumping out at me are cases where the abnormal result was already in the chart and nobody acted. Those are classic testing/follow-up problems, not primarily faulty assessment. If those are being pushed into clinician judgment categories, the whole trend line gets distorted.
turns.utterance: My hunch is that several cases that ought to be sitting in the testing phase are landing as assessment issues instead. In particular, I wonder whether the follow-up failures are being coded the way we intend.

turns.inner_thought: I think follow-up failures are already well represented because I've been using that bucket for any broken diagnostic loop after concern starts, whether it's outreach, scheduling, downstream testing, or completion. The March colon cancer cases are exactly the kind of examples I have in mind from the dashboard extract, and those supported keeping that bucket broad.
turns.utterance: I do think the follow-up failures are being captured. I've been putting broken loops into that bucket pretty consistently, and the March colon cancer cases were part of why I felt comfortable with that approach.

turns.inner_thought: That's exactly my point on those three peer-reviewed colon cancer delays: positive FIT, then delayed escalation after the result was already available. To me they're textbook examples of follow-up after an abnormal result, and clinically they should anchor the testing side, not get diluted into broader access or process language.
turns.utterance: Right, and when I think about the March colon cancer cases, those three are exactly why this stands out to me. I would have expected them to pull more clearly into the testing side, particularly under follow-up failures, rather than leaving the overall picture so weighted toward assessment.

turns.inner_thought: If I can get all pending records finalized this week, the dashboard trend will stop moving and I can issue the committee packet without another late rewrite. We do not have time for another prolonged back-and-forth after slides are drafted.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, if we can close the backlog this week, the trend line should be stable enough for the patient safety committee, and I can avoid another dashboard revision cycle.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the backlog needs attention, but I don't actually need every administrative field polished before committee. What matters is that the clinically important cases have agreed breakdown points so the testing-versus-assessment split isn't misleading. A software status of complete is not the same as true closure.
turns.utterance: I agree, we need to close the backlog. My main concern is that the major cases are resolved in a way that gives the committee a trustworthy split, so we're not presenting something that overstates assessment and understates testing.

turns.inner_thought: The cleanest fix is a standardized re-abstraction of the full flagged set. If my team does a second pass with the taxonomy from the export file, we'll have consistent field logic and an auditable trail. I need to get them started quickly if we're going to hit the report deadline.
turns.utterance: Then maybe the most practical next step is a second pass with the taxonomy on the flagged reports. My abstraction team can start as soon as I export the current batch.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a second pass should let us do targeted physician adjudication on the ambiguous and high-harm cases without redoing everything. I can ask two faculty reviewers to look at the discordant charts by Thursday so we settle the clinically important categorizations before the committee sees them.
turns.utterance: Yes, let's do a second pass with the taxonomy this week. I can also pull in two faculty reviewers to look over the major-harm and discordant cases by Thursday so we can close the backlog in a way that makes the trend more interpretable.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I'll pull the three March colorectal records from the dashboard export, rerun the broad follow-up bucket across the flagged set, and send the full re-abstraction file to the team. Once those records are finalized in RLDatix, next month's report should go out cleanly.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll pull the March colon cancer records, rerun the follow-up bucket, and send out the re-review file so we can update next month's report.
